claim: Disordered proteins and domains often assemble into condensates with polyanionic nucleic acids, primarily via charge complementarity, regulating numerous cellular functions.
source: Disordered proteins and domains often assemble into condensates with polyanionic nucleic acids, primarily via charge complementarity, regulating numerous cellular functions.
evidence: This is a general statement about disordered proteins and condensates that draws from established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: CytR forms metastable liquid-like condensates with polyP and DNA.
source: CytR forms metastable liquid-like condensates with polyP and DNA, while undergoing liquid-to-solid transition in the former and dissolving in the latter.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations including microscopy and FRAP experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: CytR undergoes liquid-to-solid transition with polyphosphate.
source: CytR forms metastable liquid-like condensates with polyP and DNA, while undergoing liquid-to-solid transition in the former and dissolving in the latter.
evidence: This is supported by time-dependent turbidity, ThT fluorescence, and FRAP measurements showing decreased recovery over time.

claim: CytR condensates with DNA dissolve over time.
source: CytR forms metastable liquid-like condensates with polyP and DNA, while undergoing liquid-to-solid transition in the former and dissolving in the latter.
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-dependent turbidity measurements and microscopy images showing droplet disappearance.

claim: Polyphosphate induces large secondary-structure changes in CytR variants.
source: Polyphosphate induces large secondary-structure changes, with two of the mutants adopting polyproline II-like structures within droplets, while DNA has only minimal structural effects.
evidence: This is supported by far-UV CD spectroscopy and FTIR measurements showing spectral changes upon polyP addition.

claim: Two CytR mutants adopt polyproline II-like structures within polyP droplets.
source: Polyphosphate induces large secondary-structure changes, with two of the mutants adopting polyproline II-like structures within droplets, while DNA has only minimal structural effects.
evidence: This is supported by SVD analysis of CD spectra showing a component with polyproline II characteristics.

claim: DNA has only minimal structural effects on CytR variants.
source: Polyphosphate induces large secondary-structure changes, with two of the mutants adopting polyproline II-like structures within droplets, while DNA has only minimal structural effects.
evidence: This is demonstrated by far-UV CD and FTIR measurements showing minimal spectral changes with DNA.

claim: Polyphosphate can more efficiently discern conformational heterogeneity in the starting protein ensemble than DNA.
source: Our findings reveal how polyphosphate can more efficiently discern conformational heterogeneity in the starting protein ensemble, its structure, and compactness, with broad implications in assembly mechanisms involving polyP and stress response in bacterial systems.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential behaviors observed with polyP versus DNA across the three CytR variants.

claim: Biomolecular condensates are mesoscale membrane-less structures that facilitate various cellular processes from stress response and signal transduction to RNA processing and chromatin organization.
source: Biomolecular condensates are mesoscale membrane-less structures that facilitate various cellular processes from stress response and signal transduction to RNA processing and chromatin organization (Brangwynne et al., 2009; Hyman and Brangwynne, 2011; Shin and Brangwynne, 2017; Banani et al., 2017; Alberti and Hyman, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Condensates are formed by the demixing or phase separation of bio-macromolecules into a polymer-rich or a condensed phase and a solvent-rich phase.
source: Physically, condensates are formed by the demixing or phase separation of bio-macromolecules (i.e. proteins, DNA, RNA) into a polymer-rich or a condensed phase and a solvent-rich phase.
evidence: This is a description of the physical basis of condensate formation based on established knowledge.

claim: Phase separation can be driven by homotypic or heterotypic interactions depending on the nature of demixing species.
source: The phase separation can be driven by homotypic or heterotypic interactions depending on the nature of demixing species, with a host of factors including the concentration and composition of constituent species, specific ions, ionic strength, temperature, and pH governing the transition (Shapiro et al., 2021; Pappu et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Disordered regions of proteins have more propensity and prevalence for forming condensates than folded regions.
source: Both folded and disordered regions of proteins can form condensates, with a lot more propensity and prevalence noted in the latter.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Biomolecular condensates are implicated in numerous diseases, specifically in neurodegenerative disorders.
source: Biomolecular condensates are also implicated in numerous diseases, and specifically in neurodegenerative disorders, with the condensates or sometimes the dilute phase proposed to seed the formation of aggregates and amyloids (Alberti and Hyman, 2021; Rai et al., 2021; Agarwal and Mukhopadhyay, 2022; Rangachari, 2023; Mukherjee et al., 2024).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Complex coacervation involves oppositely charged macromolecules condensing and promoting phase transition.
source: Complex coacervation, wherein oppositely charged macromolecules condense and promote phase transition, is often observed in DNA- and RNA-binding domains that harbor excess positive charges to bind the anionic counterpart (Pappu et al., 2023; Larson et al., 2017; Strom et al., 2017; Vieregg et al., 2018; Dutagaci et al., 2021; King and Shakya, 2021; Phan et al., 2024; Nordenskiöld et al., 2024).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The role of inorganic polyphosphates in condensate formation and maturation has been less explored.
source: However, the role of inorganic polyphosphates (polyP), a series of phosphate units (Pi) linked together via phosphoanhydride bonds (Figure 1A), in condensate formation and maturation has been less explored.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of research in the field.

claim: PolyP is a ubiquitous molecule that is produced under stress conditions in all organisms.
source: PolyP is a ubiquitous molecule that is produced under stress conditions like oxidative stress, heat shock, nutrition limitation, etc., in all organisms (Kornberg et al., 1999; Brown and Kornberg, 2004; Rao et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The polymer length of polyP varies among different species, ranging from a few tens to thousands.
source: In fact, the polymer length of polyP and the concentration vary among different species, ranging from a few tens to thousands, reaching up to 50 mM in bacterial cells under stress conditions (Kornberg et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: PolyP concentration can reach up to 50 mM in bacterial cells under stress conditions.
source: In fact, the polymer length of polyP and the concentration vary among different species, ranging from a few tens to thousands, reaching up to 50 mM in bacterial cells under stress conditions (Kornberg et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: PolyP has been implicated in numerous processes ranging from modulation of nucleoid structure to biofilm formation.
source: Apart from the stress response, it has been implicated in numerous processes ranging from modulation of nucleoid structure to biofilm formation (Shi et al., 2004; Xie et al., 2019; Müller et al., 2019; Beaufay et al., 2020; Beaufay et al., 2021; Solesio et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: PolyP is able to act both as a chaperone and in promoting aggregation.
source: Intriguingly, polyP is able to act both as a chaperone (Gray et al., 2014) (assisting folding of proteins, preventing protein misfolding and inhibiting aggregation) and in promoting aggregation (Cremers et al., 2016; Yoo et al., 2018), indicative of more complex underlying mechanisms (Xie and Jakob, 2019; Guan and Jakob, 2024) which could be protein specific.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: CytR DBD is an intrinsically disordered domain that adopts a folded conformation in the presence of DNA.
source: Here, we employ Cytidine repressor DBD (CytR DBD or CytR or CytR wildtype), an intrinsically disordered domain (Figure 1B, C) that adopts a folded conformation in the presence of DNA (Moody et al., 2011) as a model system to answer these questions.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature and references to figures showing disorder propensity.

claim: The WT CytR populates a minor excited state which is fully folded (~8–10%).
source: Specifically, the WT populates a minor excited state which is fully folded (~8–10%), but otherwise the native ensemble is disordered, with marginal helicity and a Stokes radius of 19.5 Å (green in Figure 1D, F; Munshi et al., 2018c; Madhurima et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature and references to experimental data in figures.

claim: The WT CytR native ensemble is disordered, with marginal helicity and a Stokes radius of 19.5 Å.
source: Specifically, the WT populates a minor excited state which is fully folded (~8–10%), but otherwise the native ensemble is disordered, with marginal helicity and a Stokes radius of 19.5 Å (green in Figure 1D, F; Munshi et al., 2018c; Madhurima et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by CD spectroscopy and Stokes radius measurements shown in Figure 1D and F.

claim: The DM mutant (A29V/A48M) displays properties of a fully folded compact domain driven by enhanced hydrophobicity.
source: One of the mutants we consider is the double mutant of CytR (A29V/A48M; DM) which displays the properties of a fully folded compact domain driven by the enhanced hydrophobicity of the side chains at positions 29 and 48; these two mutations act synergistically to switch the ensemble from being disordered to fully ordered as shown earlier (Munshi et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The DM mutant displays a higher helicity and lower Stokes radius of 17 Å compared to the WT.
source: The DM therefore displays a higher helicity and lower Stokes radius of 17 Å, compared to the WT (blue in Figure 1D, F).
evidence: This is supported by CD spectroscopy and Stokes radius measurements shown in Figure 1D and F.

claim: The P33A mutant eliminates the minor folded state population because of the enhanced flexibility of alanine in place of proline.
source: The other mutant is P33A, in which the minor folded state population is eliminated because of the enhanced flexibility of alanine in the place of proline (Munshi et al., 2018c).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The P33A mutant is nearly fully disordered with a Stokes radius of 21.5 Å and minimum helicity.
source: The P33A mutant is nearly fully disordered as evidenced by the Stokes radius of 21.5 Å and minimum helicity (red in Figure 1D, F).
evidence: This is supported by CD spectroscopy and Stokes radius measurements shown in Figure 1D and F.

claim: CytR has an excess charge of +9 and a large positive electrostatic potential in its folded conformation.
source: In addition, because CytR has an excess charge of +9 and a large positive electrostatic potential in its folded conformation (Figure 1G), it binds non-specifically to DNA (Munshi et al., 2018b; Munshi et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by electrostatic potential calculations shown in Figure 1G and citations to prior literature.

claim: CytR binds non-specifically to DNA.
source: In addition, because CytR has an excess charge of +9 and a large positive electrostatic potential in its folded conformation (Figure 1G), it binds non-specifically to DNA (Munshi et al., 2018b; Munshi et al., 2018a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Solutions containing [WT] > 25 μM and [polyP] > 10 μM consistently showed higher turbidity.
source: Solutions containing [WT] > 25 μM and [polyP] > 10 μM consistently showed higher turbidity (turbidity at 350 nm).
evidence: This is based on turbidity measurements shown in the phase diagram (Figure 2A).

claim: DIC microscopy reveals droplet-shaped condensates with a diameter of ~1–4 μm on average for WT with polyP.
source: DIC (differential interference contrast) microscopy reveals droplet-shaped condensates with a diameter of ~1–4 μm on average (Figure 2B; also vide infra), which is also confirmed by fluorescence microscopy of NHS-rhodamine-labeled protein (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on microscopy images shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: The number of droplets increases with increasing [WT] in the range between 25 and 90 μM.
source: The number of droplets increases with increasing [WT] in the range between 25 and 90 μM consistent with OD measurements (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The interaction between CytR and polyP is expected to be driven by non-specific electrostatic interactions.
source: Given that CytR carries a large excess positive charge (+9) and polyP is an anionic polymer with no structural preference (unlike DNA), the interaction and the resultant assembly process is expected to be driven by non-specific electrostatic interactions.
evidence: This is inferred from the charge properties of CytR and polyP.

claim: The OD of WT-polyP mixtures is independent of ionic strength until ~80 mM, following which it linearly decreases with near-zero turbidity at 200 mM.
source: The OD is observed to be independent of ionic strength until ~80 mM following which it linearly decreases with near-zero turbidity at 200 mM (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on ionic strength-dependent turbidity measurements shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Under physiological ionic strength conditions of 150–160 mM, the OD value is still ~0.6 with droplets evident in fluorescence microscopy.
source: Under physiological ionic strength conditions of 150–160 mM, the OD value is still ~0.6 and with droplets evident in fluorescence microscopy (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on turbidity measurements and microscopy images shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The P33A mutant aggregates on addition of polyP.
source: The double mutant (DM), which is folded and compact, also undergoes spontaneous phase separation at the same concentrations as the WT when mixed with polyP, while the P33A mutant aggregates on addition of polyP (Figure 2F, G).
evidence: This is based on microscopy images shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The fluorescence of NHS-rhodamine-labeled WT and DM recovers on photobleaching, highlighting the liquid-like nature of the condensates.
source: The fluorescence of the NHS-rhodamine-labeled WT and DM recovers on photobleaching, highlighting the liquid-like nature of the condensates (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is based on FRAP experiments shown in Figure 2H and 2I.

claim: Multiple coalescence and de-coalescence events are observed in both WT and DM proteins at the earliest times.
source: We also observe multiple coalescence and de-coalescence events in both the proteins at the earliest times (Figure 2J, Figure 2—video 1 for WT and Figure 2—video 2 for the DM).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse microscopy images shown in Figure 2J and videos.

claim: Charge composition and patterning alone do not determine the phase separation tendencies in the CytR-polyP system.
source: These results indicate that charge composition and patterning alone do not determine the phase separation tendencies in this system.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mutants with identical charge composition show different behaviors (phase separation vs aggregation).

claim: The starting ensemble and the population of partially structured substates are important in determining the nature of the assembly process observed.
source: They underscore the importance of the starting ensemble, and potentially the population of partially structured substates, in determining the nature of the assembly process observed.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential behaviors observed across the three CytR variants with different structural properties.

claim: The OD of WT–polyP mixtures decreases from 1.2 to less than 0.9 in the first 10 min with little increase in ThT fluorescence.
source: The OD of WT–polyP mixtures shows a strong time dependence, with the OD decreasing from 1.2 to less than 0.9 in the first 10 min, but with little increase in ThT fluorescence (left panel in Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on time-dependent turbidity and ThT fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ThT fluorescence of WT-polyP mixtures starts to increase in a sigmoidal fashion from 20 min.
source: However, the ThT fluorescence starts to increase in a sigmoidal fashion from 20 min.
evidence: This is based on time-dependent ThT fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The WT–polyP mixture forms condensates and matures into aggregates within 3 hr.
source: The WT–polyP mixture therefore forms condensates and matures into aggregates within 3 hr which is directly observable in microscopy images (Figure 3B), mirroring reports in numerous other systems that undergo droplet formation followed by a liquid-to-solid phase transition (Patel et al., 2015; Ray et al., 2020; Shen et al., 2023; Gracia et al., 2022; Dhakal et al., 2023).
evidence: This is based on time-dependent turbidity, ThT fluorescence, and microscopy images shown in Figure 3A and 3B, and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: Control experiments with protein alone did not reveal any changes in turbidity or aggregation in the entire 24-hr duration.
source: Control experiments with protein alone did not reveal any changes in turbidity or aggregation in the entire 24-hr duration (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), pointing to a process entirely driven by polyP–protein interactions.
evidence: This is based on control experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The OD of the DM–polyP mixture decreases starting from a value of ~1, extending beyond 3 hr, with the OD dropping to a value of ~0.1 at the longest time points.
source: The OD of the DM–polyP mixture exhibits a similar decrease in OD starting from a value of ~1, but this trend extends beyond 3 hr, with the OD dropping to a value of ~0.1 at the longest time points (middle panel in Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on time-dependent turbidity measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The DM forms condensates with polyP that slowly dissolve with time.
source: These observations point to a scenario wherein the DM forms condensates to start with, but which slowly dissolve with time (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is inferred from the decreasing OD and microscopy images shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The P33A mutant forms only aggregates with polyP as evidenced by high OD and high ThT fluorescence across all time points in the 24-hr observation window.
source: On the other hand, the P33A mutant forms only aggregates as evidenced by the high OD and high ThT fluorescence across all time points in the 24-hr observation window (right panel in Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is based on time-dependent turbidity, ThT fluorescence, and microscopy images shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: In the WT-polyP system, the FRAP recovery amplitude decreases from 0.92 ± 0.11 at the zeroth minute to just 0.43 ± 0.04 at 60 min.
source: In the WT, the recovery amplitude decreases from 0.92 ± 0.11 at the zeroth minute to just 0.43 ± 0.04 at 60 min (Figure 3C, D).
evidence: This is based on FRAP experiments shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: The DM–polyP condensates recover near fully even at the first hour, with the recovery time slowing down by a factor of 2.
source: Alternately, the DM–polyP condensates recover near fully even at the first hour, with the recovery time slowing down by a factor of 2 (Figure 3F–H).
evidence: This is based on FRAP experiments shown in Figure 3F-H.

claim: The WT circular dichroism spectrum in the dilute phase is characterized by minima at 202 and 222 nm with ~17% of residual helical content.
source: The WT circular dichroism (CD) spectrum in the dilute phase (i.e. in the absence of polyP) is characterized by minima at 202 and 222 nm with ~17% of residual helical content (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on CD spectroscopy measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Upon formation of condensates with polyP, the WT CD spectral shape shifts substantially to one with a minimum at 230 nm and with no spectral features at wavelengths <215 nm.
source: Upon formation of condensates, the spectral shape shifts substantially to one with a minimum at 230 nm and with no spectral features at wavelengths <215 nm (Figure 4A), demonstrating that the WT adopts a non-helical and potentially an unfolded conformation in the condensed phase at initial times.
evidence: This is based on CD spectroscopy measurements shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The WT adopts a non-helical and potentially an unfolded conformation in the condensed phase with polyP at initial times.
source: Upon formation of condensates, the spectral shape shifts substantially to one with a minimum at 230 nm and with no spectral features at wavelengths <215 nm (Figure 4A), demonstrating that the WT adopts a non-helical and potentially an unfolded conformation in the condensed phase at initial times.
evidence: This is inferred from the CD spectral changes shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The DM spectrum is more representative of a folded protein with minima at both 208 and 222 nm, with the signal at 222 nm indicative of a protein with nearly 30% helical content.
source: The spectrum of DM is more representative of a folded protein with minima at both 208 and 222 nm (Figure 1D), and with the signal at 222 nm indicative of a protein with nearly 30% helical content.
evidence: This is based on CD spectroscopy measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: On mixing DM with polyP, the spectral shift resembles that of the WT, indicative of a structural change in the condensed phase.
source: On mixing with polyP, the spectral shift resembles that of the WT (Figure 4B), again indicative of a structural change in the condensed phase.
evidence: This is based on CD spectroscopy measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The P33A mutant exhibits a more intense CD spectrum with a minimum at 225 nm which is representative of β-sheet-like structures.
source: The P33A mutant, which is more unfolded (helicity ~10%), however, exhibits a more intense spectrum with a minimum at 225 nm which is representative of β-sheet-like structures (Figure 4C; see below).
evidence: This is based on CD spectroscopy measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The first two SVD components of the CD spectral time series contribute 92% of the overall signal change.
source: The first two components contribute 92% of the overall signal change (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on SVD analysis of CD spectra shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The first SVD component is the spectrum of an α-helix with clear minimum at 222 nm and another at 208 nm, and accounts for 71% of the signal change.
source: Of this, the first component is the spectrum of an α-helix with clear minimum at 222 nm and another at 208 nm, and accounts for 71% of the signal change.
evidence: This is based on SVD analysis of CD spectra shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The amplitude of the helical SVD component decreases with time in the WT and P33A variant, implying that helical conformations are less favored in their assemblies.
source: The amplitude of this component decreases with time in the WT and P33A variant, implying that helical conformations are less favored in their assemblies; this feature also signals the population of an alternate structural form which is observable in the second component (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on SVD analysis of CD spectra shown in Figure 4F.

claim: In the DM, the amplitude of the helical SVD component increases with time as expected when the droplet dissolves due to preferential transport into the dilute phase.
source: In the DM, the amplitude of the helical component increases with time as expected when the droplet dissolves due to preferential transport into the dilute phase.
evidence: This is inferred from the SVD analysis of CD spectra shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The helical content of DM recovers to just ~15% at 4 hr, conceivably due to non-specific interaction with polyP resulting in partially structured states or due to a small fraction of oligomers.
source: However, the helical content recovers to just ~15% at 4 hr (Figure 4F), conceivably due to non-specific interaction with polyP resulting in partially structured states or due to a small fraction of oligomers.
evidence: This is inferred from the SVD analysis of CD spectra shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The second SVD component, accounting for 21% of the signal change, bears the features of polyproline II structures in unfolded conformations with a maximum at 231 nm and a minimum at 207 nm.
source: The second component, accounting for 21% of the signal change, bears the features of polyproline II structures in unfolded conformations (Shi et al., 2002) with a maximum at 231 nm and a minimum at 207 nm (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on SVD analysis of CD spectra shown in Figure 4E and is supported by a citation.

claim: There is a marginal increase in the amplitude of the second SVD component in the WT in the first hour, following which it stabilizes.
source: There is a marginal increase in the amplitude of this component in the WT in the first hour, following which it stabilizes (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is based on SVD analysis of CD spectra shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The amplitude of the second SVD component increases in the DM continuously even at 4 hr indicating a tussle between the helical and polyproline II-like structures.
source: The amplitude of this component increases in the DM continuously even at 4 hr indicating a tussle between the helical and polyproline II-like structures (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is inferred from the SVD analysis of CD spectra shown in Figure 4G.

claim: In the P33A variant, the amplitude of the second SVD component has a negative sign, pointing to a strong contribution from β-turn or polyproline I conformations, mixed with β-sheet.
source: In the P33A variant, the amplitude of the second component has a negative sign, and when multiplied with the second component (required for reconstructing the original spectra), it points to a strong contribution from β-turn or polyproline I conformations, mixed with β-sheet (Kelly and Price, 2000).
evidence: This is inferred from the SVD analysis of CD spectra and is supported by a citation.

claim: Both the WT and the DM 'unfold' on forming condensates with polyP, with polyproline II-rich structures observed at longer times (~1–2 hr) in both the mixtures.
source: In summary, we find that both the WT and the DM 'unfold' on forming condensates with polyP, with polyproline II-rich structures observed at longer times (~1–2 hr) in both the mixtures.
evidence: This is inferred from the CD and SVD analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: The condensates formed by WT and DM with polyP are metastable, either undergoing a liquid-to-solid transition as in the WT or partially dissolving with time as in the DM.
source: The condensates thus formed are metastable, either undergoing a liquid-to-solid transition as in the WT or partially dissolving with time as in the DM.
evidence: This is inferred from the time-dependent turbidity, ThT fluorescence, and FRAP measurements presented in Figure 3.

claim: At the 4-hr time point, the DM acquires helical character due to the partial dissolution of the condensates, while the WT forms only aggregates.
source: At the 4-hr time point, however, the DM acquires helical character due to the partial dissolution of the condensates, while the WT forms only aggregates.
evidence: This is inferred from the CD spectroscopy and SVD analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: The starting ensemble determines the extent of metastability and the maturation of condensates, and not just the nature of assemblies formed.
source: The starting ensemble thus determines the extent of metastability and the maturation of condensates, and not just the nature of assemblies formed.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential behaviors observed across the three CytR variants.

claim: CytR WT forms condensates with just 1 μM of double-stranded DNA in a concentration-dependent manner at 20 mM phosphate buffer, pH 7.
source: We find that CytR WT also forms condensates with just 1 μM of double-stranded DNA in a concentration-dependent manner at 20 mM phosphate buffer, pH 7 (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This is based on turbidity measurements and microscopy images shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Both the DM and the P33A variants form phase-separated condensates with DNA, unlike aggregated assemblies observed with polyP-P33A droplets.
source: Both the DM and the P33A variants form phase-separated condensates with DNA (Figure 5F, G), unlike aggregated assemblies observed with polyP-P33A droplets (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is based on microscopy images shown in Figure 5F and 5G, compared to Figure 2G.

claim: The condensates with DNA dissolve within 90 min in both the WT and DM.
source: The time-dependent properties of the condensates with DNA again differ from those of polyP: the condensates dissolve within 90 min in both the WT and DM (Figure 5H, I), while taking nearly 3 hr for the P33A variant (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on time-dependent turbidity measurements and microscopy images shown in Figure 5H, 5I, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The P33A-DNA condensates take nearly 3 hr to dissolve.
source: The time-dependent properties of the condensates with DNA again differ from those of polyP: the condensates dissolve within 90 min in both the WT and DM (Figure 5H, I), while taking nearly 3 hr for the P33A variant (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on time-dependent turbidity measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Numerous WT-DNA droplets with a mean size of 1.6 µm form within the first few minutes, which coalesce to form larger droplets of size 2–3 µm, following which they dissolve.
source: Numerous droplets with a mean size of 1.6 µm form within the first few minutes (Figure 5J), which coalesce to form larger droplets of size 2–3 µm, following which they dissolve.
evidence: This is based on droplet size distribution analysis shown in Figure 5J.

claim: OD is less sensitive to droplet formation with DNA, as droplets are observed even at 3 hr when the OD is effectively zero.
source: We find that OD is less sensitive to droplet formation with DNA, as we do observe few droplets even at 3 hr, a time point at which the OD is effectively zero (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on turbidity measurements and microscopy images shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both the DM and P33A mutants recover fully (amplitudes ~1) with similar half-times compared to the WT at 60 min in DNA condensates.
source: Both the DM and P33A mutants recover fully (amplitudes ~1) and with similar half-times compared to the WT at 60 min (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on FRAP experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The trends with DNA are identical at 11.2 µM DNA (equivalent negative charges to 22 µM polyP) compared to lower DNA concentration.
source: To rule out the possibility of concentration differences (22 µM for polyP and 1 µM for DNA) contributing to the observed diverse behavior across the two anionic polymers, we carried out a set of control experiments at 11.2 µM DNA, a concentration at which the number of negative charges is equivalent to that of 22 µM polyP. However, the trends were identical to those observed at lower DNA concentration (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), further underscoring that the differences in chemical and conformational properties of the anionic polymers contribute to the diverse assembly behaviors.
evidence: This is based on control experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The absence of large structural change or aging into an aggregate with time in DNA condensates is evident in FTIR spectra which do not change significantly.
source: The absence of large structural change or aging into an aggregate with time is also evident in FTIR spectra which do not change significantly (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on FTIR spectroscopy measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: The WT displays 50% less negative CD signal at ~202–204 nm which shifts to longer wavelength after the first hour, indicating helical structure acquisition.
source: The WT, however, does display 50% less negative signal at ~202–204 nm which shifts to longer wavelength after the first hour (blue and green spectra in Figure 5L), indicating helical structure acquisition and mirroring earlier reports (Moody et al., 2011; Munshi et al., 2018c).
evidence: This is based on CD spectroscopy measurements shown in Figure 5L and is supported by citations.

claim: PolyP spontaneously induces aggregation in FruR.
source: PolyP spontaneously induces aggregation in FruR, while the molten-globular variant forms condensates but only at the earliest times (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This is based on turbidity, ThT fluorescence, and microscopy measurements shown in Figure 6B-D.

claim: The molten-globular FruR Y19A variant forms condensates with polyP but only at the earliest times.
source: PolyP spontaneously induces aggregation in FruR, while the molten-globular variant forms condensates but only at the earliest times (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This is based on turbidity, ThT fluorescence, and microscopy measurements shown in Figure 6B-D.

claim: The intensity of ThT fluorescence in FruR–polyP mixture increases with time, indicating that polyP induces a time-dependent enhanced aggregation of FruR.
source: The intensity of ThT fluorescence protein–polyP mixture increases with time, indicating that polyP induces a time-dependent enhanced aggregation of FruR, while the FruR Y19A–polyP mixture undergoes a rapid liquid-to-solid transition within the first 20 min (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on ThT fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The FruR Y19A–polyP mixture undergoes a rapid liquid-to-solid transition within the first 20 min.
